speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, I beg to move. "That the total sum to be allocated for Head E of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, I wish to focus on the challenges of litigants who do not have lawyers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will highlight cases from the ground to illustrate difficulties they face in normal times and in COVID-19 times.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the onset, I wish to acknowledge the attention that the Courts have been paying to the litigants in person.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are training programmes at the Singapore Judicial College to sensitise judges on how to handle such litigants in Court.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lawyers also see judges going the extra mile to explain to unrepresented persons, the requirements of the law and legal procedure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are also inquiry counters at the Courts and education brochures in the four official languages.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My purpose is not to criticise current efforts but to highlight some observations from the ground for the Courts' consideration for possible further enhancements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are three main challenges I wish to highlight.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, the need for public buy in of Court procedures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is common at my Meet-the-People sessions to encounter Chinese-speaking residents showing me court documents and saying that they are unable to read them and do not know what they should do next.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that court interpreters can be applied for in advance of court hearings, and are available for Mandarin, Malay and Tamil, and other specific languages and dialects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, this has to be applied for through e-litigation in advance, otherwise, deployment will be subject to availability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder if many litigants in person have used e-litigation to apply for such interpretation services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for court documents, they are issued in English.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Residents sometimes tell me that they do not understand the contents of Orders made by the courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If this is not possible for all documents, then is it possible at least for court orders, so that litigants are clear what is required of them?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second point is the need for public buy in of Court procedures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate the point, I note some unhappiness from residents who had their neighbour disputes adjudicated by the CDRT which was discussed in the earlier Committee of Supply debate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The unhappiness was both about the hearing and the outcome.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I would hope that CDRT judges are specially selected with empathy and patience as key traits, and also have the ability to explain issues to litigants in simple and vernacular language.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for the Orders made by the CDRT, some residents are shocked to be ordered to stay out of their homes for a few weeks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After all, this is a most drastic order that undermines their property rights.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The courts had to close for several weeks during the circuit breaker and continues to restrict physical hearings and counter services.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There must now be a significant backlog of cases due to COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While some hearings took place via remote means such as Zoom, I wonder how many litigants in person had the resources and the wherewithal to avail themselves of that option.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He was conducting a civil claim for damages after a road accident which left him partially disabled.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After obtaining interlocutory judgment, his next step to quantify his damages was delayed due to court closures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: An application by him was dismissed by the court remotely and he did not understand why.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I am grateful to Ms Lim for recognising some of the efforts to handle litigants-in-persons in court.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both my Ministry and the Judiciary remain committed to ensuring access to justice for all.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And indeed, one of the guiding principles of the Civil Justice Reform Committee established by MinLaw was to advance access to justice for all persons, including litigants-in-person and SMEs.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we are simplifying and streamlining legal processes and designing them with the ultimate end-users in mind.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Cases can take a judge-led approach where appropriate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we are leveraging on technology to make legal processes more accessible and convenient, and to channel timely and useful information to those facing legal issues, especially litigants-in-person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, the Community Justice Centre (CJC)’s Automated Court Document Assembly System (ACDA).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a free online service that provides step-by-step guidance to generate and file certain court forms, such as applying for deputyship, which a lay person can do on his own.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If necessary, court staff will also be available on hand to assist.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, we have taken steps to enhance awareness and also support structures to help litigants-in-person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I spoke earlier about the improvements that we are making to legal aid for civil and criminal matters, to support litigants of limited means who are unable to afford their own lawyers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Community Justice Centre (CJC) also runs a one-stop HELP (Helping to Empower Litigants-in-Person) Centre.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These provide support services such as free on-site legal advice, and also emotional and psychological support through the Friends of Litigants-in-Person (FLIP) scheme.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Elderly or less well-educated persons ought not feel intimidated or apprehensive in participating in legal proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ample support is available to help them navigate the court process.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the litigant struggles with English, the Community Justice Centre will endeavour to source for volunteers who are conversant in other languages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For litigants-in-person who require a court interpreter, they can make a written request, and the reason to have to make the written request in advance is obviously the number of intepreters might be limited.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If all go for a Mandarin speaker or a dialect speaker on the same day, there needs to be an allocation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But to the extent possible, the courts will allocate the appropriate interpreter to ensure that the process can take place.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that the individuals who do not understand English can still continue to take part in the proceedings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Certainly, the Judge will not proceed with a hearing, if one party is unable to follow the proceedings due to language difficulties.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim asked about the translation of court documents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For cases before the Community Courts and Tribunals, or cases involving simple court Orders, litigants-in-persons who need assistance understanding court correspondence may call the court's hotline.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They will be assisted by staff who can explain the content of documents to them either over the phone, or on occasion, in person when they meet.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For other cases, if a translation is required, litigants can be referred to third parties who provide translation services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are in the midst of exploring with the CDCs and with LSPBS, a range of options to assist litigants who need assistance who have English court documents, and the avenues being considered are platforms to explain the documents verbally in a language that the litigant is comfortable with, providing advice where needed, as you heard Ms Hany Soh explain earlier, or in certain cases, assisting with the cost of engaging translation services, where needed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim raised some questions on the impact of COVID-19 on the Courts and litigants-in-person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some amount of disruption in the past year has been unavoidable due to the need to combat the spread of COVID-19 to save lives and the pandemic has had an immense impact not only on court processes but really on all aspects of our daily lives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There has been some backlog and the State Courts have lost a number of hearing days due to the vacation of hearings because of the circuit breaker period – likewise, the Family Justice Courts as well as the High Courts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As far as remote hearings, and more generally, the increased usage of technology in the Courts are concerned, MinLaw and the Courts are keenly sensitive to the needs of court users who are not represented and less technologically inclined.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim asked whether litigants-in-person have the resources to use Zoom.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They can do so on their own if necessary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Alternatively, those who require assistance can receive assistance through telephone or over the counter, on online live-chat or through email communications.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim raised the case of her resident who was looking at quantification of damages.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This resident can avail himself of any of the above measures that I have mentioned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In addition, the litigant can also write to the Court Registry to explain the situation, ask for an earlier hearing date and they can do so through any of the various modes I have mentioned.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I spoke earlier about how MinLaw is working with agencies to review the Community Dispute Management Framework (CDMF).

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Community Disputes Resolution Tribunal (CDRT) cases are heard by District Judges who are designated as Tribunal Judges.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: They are empowered to handle cases in a less adversarial way and to ensure that proceedings are simple for litigants to navigate.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The CDRT is not bound by the rules of evidence and proceedings are designed to be judge-led.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These judges are trained in mediation and they continue to assist in every case, assess each case and assess the parties for suitability in mediation even as the case proceeds on an adversarial basis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If, despite all these measures, after exhausting all attempts at an amicable solution, there is still a dispute, then the CDRT will have to make a decision and issue an order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These orders then have to be complied with.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ms Lim spoke about the residents' concern, that they can ordered to stay out of their homes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: What Ms Lim refers to are Exclusion Orders (EO), which require the respondent to temporarily move out from his place of residence.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, the CDRT must consider the impact of the order on the contravening party and any other individual who may be reasonably affected by the order.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Access to justice, Sir, remains a key cornerstone of the Ministry and we will continue to advance our efforts in this regard.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We thank Ms Lim for her feedback and suggestions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: One clarification for the Minister concerning my suggestion on the translation of court orders into other languages.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: In his response, he mentioned that there were avenues available through staff or perhaps through the CDC network to explain verbally to the resident the contents of the orders.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I wonder if he will agree with me that having a written translation is certainly something that is a better and stronger reference point for the resident, because sometimes when people talk to you, you cannot retain the information or you remember inaccurately, whereas if you have a translated document, you can refer to it and it is, in a sense, a more reliable source.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That said, I think, through various means, we want to ensure that the litigants-in-person are able to understand the process, understand what the judge is saying, what the other party is seeking to achieve.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This, I think, upholds the integrity of the process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will take these necessary steps to ensure that litigants-in-person will be able to understand the process through a variety of means.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Lim, would you like to withdraw the amendment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Mr Chairman, it is good to hear the Courts' continuing commitment to justice for all, especially litigants-in-person, and I would highly urge that the Courts continue in this direction to address any gaps.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: With that, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
